title: In 1893, He Stitched Around a Beating Heart.

brand.cta: Follow The Black History Room for one story a day.

beats.text: He operated beside a beating heart.
Born in Pennsylvania in 1856, a barber's son, he worked as a shoemaker's apprentice and a barber.
In 1883, he graduated from Chicago Medical College.
Black patients were turned away, and Black nurses had nowhere to train. So in 1891, he opened Provident Hospital.
One summer night in 1893, a young man named James Cornish was carried in, stabbed in the chest.
With no X-rays and no transfusions, Williams opened his chest and sewed the torn sac around his heart, as it beat.
Fifty-one days later, Cornish walked out. He lived for more than twenty years.
It was one of the first successful operations of its kind in America.
He went on to run Freedmen's Hospital in Washington, and became the first Black member of the American College of Surgeons.
A barber's son stitched around a beating heart. His patient walked out alive.

facts.claim: Born Hollidaysburg, PA, 1856 (Columbia: 1858); son of a barber; shoemaker's apprentice and barber.
May 1891 opened Provident Hospital and Training School for Nurses, interracial staff.
July 1893, James Cornish, 24, stabbed in the chest.
Opened the chest and sutured the torn pericardium while the heart was beating.
Cornish left after 51 days (30 Aug) and lived 20+ more years.
Second known successful pericardium suture in the US (Henry Dalton, 1891, was first).
Chief surgeon, Freedmen's Hospital 1894; first/only Black charter member of the American College of Surgeons 1913.

notUsed: 'First open-heart surgery': not accurate (Dalton 1891 earlier; Rehn 1896 sutured the heart muscle); the reel says 'one of the first'
'No X-rays': X-rays were discovered in 1895, so true by definition; transfusions were not yet possible
